stem: A block has 8 transactions. How many hashes, including leaves and root, does its Merkle tree contain?
explanation: 8 leaves + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 nodes, i.e. 2n − 1. 16 would need a ninth leaf.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A Bitcoin block has 5 transactions. How does Bitcoin form the next Merkle level from the odd leaf?
options: It duplicates the last hash to pair it
It hashes the fifth alone into the root
It pairs the fifth with the first
explanation: Bitcoin repeats the final hash when a level has an odd count. Dropping or wrapping would change the commitment rules.
concept: Odd level: duplicate the last hash.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An attacker controls 10% of hash power. Using the simplified (q/p)^z catch-up bound, what is the chance of reversing 6 confirmations?
explanation: (0.1/0.9)^6 = (1/9)^6 ≈ 1.9 × 10⁻⁶. The probability falls exponentially with each confirmation.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Alice reuses one address for every payment. What is the main privacy consequence?
options: Anyone can total and link all her receipts
Her private key becomes public on the ledger
explanation: A reused address ties all activity together on the public ledger. Fresh addresses per payment make linking harder; the key stays private either way.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why does a 51% attacker still fail to steal coins from Bob's address?
options: The attacker cannot mine new blocks once Bob's coins confirm
Spending needs Bob's signature, which hash power cannot forge
explanation: Majority hash power lets the attacker reorder or censor, but every valid spend still needs Bob's private key. They can only double-spend their own coins.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A Merkle proof is given for transaction T in block B. What does it NOT prove?
options: That T is included in block B
That T hashes up to B's Merkle root
That T is the only spend of its inputs
explanation: Inclusion and integrity follow from the path to the root; uniqueness of spends needs full validation of the chain. Light clients rely on miners for that.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: As the subsidy shrinks toward zero, what must sustain miner incentives?
explanation: Once issuance ends, fees are the only revenue securing the chain. Bitcoin has no staking reward.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A wallet holds UTXOs of 0.4, 0.7 and 1.1 BTC and must pay 1.0 BTC with minimal inputs. Which does it spend?
explanation: One input of 1.1 covers 1.0 plus fee with change; 0.4 + 0.7 also works but uses two inputs. 0.7 alone is too small.
concept: Coin selection: fewest inputs that cover the payment.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why do Bitcoin nodes reject a block whose coinbase claims 7 BTC at a 3.125 BTC subsidy with 1 BTC of fees?
options: The block lacks a Merkle root
Fees cannot be claimed by miners
explanation: The coinbase may claim at most 3.125 + 1 = 4.125 BTC. Validity rules are enforced by every full node, whatever the miner's hash power.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which change to a block would NOT alter its Merkle root?
explanation: The nonce is in the header, outside the transaction tree. Order, amounts and membership all change leaf hashes.
concept: Merkle root covers transactions, not header fields.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Fees are 20 satoshi per byte. What is the fee on a 250-byte transaction in BTC?
explanation: 250 × 20 = 5,000 satoshi = 0.00005 BTC (1 BTC = 10⁸ satoshi). The other options slip a decimal place.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Two miners find valid blocks at the same height. How is the fork resolved?
options: Nodes follow whichever branch gains more cumulative work
The block with the earlier timestamp wins permanently
The block with the lower nonce wins
explanation: The next block decides which branch is heavier; the other block becomes stale and its transactions return to the mempool. Timestamps and nonces do not decide.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A shop accepts 0-confirmation payments for coffee but waits 6 for laptops. Assess the policy.
options: Wrong: confirmations do not affect risk
Wasteful: one confirmation is always final
Sensible: confirmations scale with value at risk
explanation: Small payments tolerate double-spend risk for speed; large ones justify waiting as reversal risk falls exponentially. No single rule fits all values.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A designer proposes putting all transaction hashes directly in the header instead of a Merkle root. Best critique?
options: Headers grow with transaction count and light clients lose short proofs
It would make the chain more secure by exposing every hash
It removes the need for signatures
It is identical to a Merkle root
explanation: A Merkle root keeps the header fixed at 80 bytes and inclusion proofs logarithmic. A flat list loses both benefits.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Design a payment flow for a merchant receiving many small Bitcoin payments privately. Which is best?
options: One public address reused for all customers to simplify reconciliation
Accept only payments with zero fees
A fresh address per invoice from an HD wallet, settled in batches
Ask customers to email their private keys
explanation: HD wallets derive fresh addresses, limiting linkability, and batching reduces fees. Address reuse harms privacy and private keys are never shared.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In a BFT system of n = 3f + 1 nodes, how many Byzantine nodes can be tolerated?
explanation: With n = 3f + 1, up to f nodes may be arbitrary while 2f + 1 honest votes still form a quorum. n/2 applies to crash faults with majority quorums.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How many crash-faulty nodes can a Raft cluster of 2f + 1 nodes tolerate?
explanation: A majority of f + 1 remains to elect a leader and commit. Raft does not tolerate Byzantine nodes.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is a Sybil attack?
options: Creating many fake identities to gain influence
Delaying all network messages to stall block production
explanation: In open systems, identities are free, so votes per identity fail. PoW and PoS tie influence to a scarce resource instead.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does 'safety' mean for a consensus protocol?
options: Honest nodes never finalise conflicting states
The network never goes offline, even during partitions
explanation: Safety is 'nothing bad happens'; liveness is 'something good eventually happens'. A protocol may pause yet stay safe.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How often does Bitcoin retarget its difficulty?
explanation: 2,016 blocks is about two weeks at 10 minutes. 210,000 blocks is the halving interval.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: If the target is lowered, what happens to difficulty?
explanation: A smaller target accepts fewer hashes, so more attempts are needed. Difficulty and target are inversely related.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How long is an Ethereum slot?
explanation: A slot is 12 s; an epoch is 32 slots = 6.4 minutes. 10 minutes is Bitcoin's block time.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How much ETH backs one standard validator?
explanation: Each standard validator deposits 32 ETH into the deposit contract. Smaller holders use pools or delegation.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which Ethereum offence is slashable?
options: Being offline for a full epoch during maintenance
Signing two different blocks for one slot
explanation: Provable equivocation is slashed; being offline only incurs inactivity penalties. Client choice is not an offence.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why does PoET still require trust?
options: It uses proof of work underneath
It relies on trusted hardware attesting the wait time
It reveals validators' private keys to the network for checks
explanation: Intel SGX attestation proves a node waited; compromise the enclave and the lottery breaks. That trust replaces energy expenditure.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In DPoS, who produces blocks?
options: The miner with the most hash power
A small elected set of delegates
explanation: Token holders vote in, for example, 21 producers who take turns. This raises throughput but concentrates power.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What distinguishes LPoS from DPoS?
options: LPoS replaces staking with proof of work by lessees
Leased stake never leaves the owner's wallet
explanation: In LPoS the owner leases staking power to a node but keeps custody and can revoke. DPoS elects a fixed producer set by vote.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A BFT network has 10 replicas. How many Byzantine replicas can it tolerate?
explanation: n ≥ 3f + 1 gives f ≤ (10 − 1)/3 = 3. Four would need 13 replicas.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A BFT network must tolerate 4 Byzantine nodes. What minimum quorum must agree?
explanation: n = 3·4 + 1 = 13 and quorum = 2f + 1 = 9. 5 of 9 is a crash-fault majority.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A target requires the first 20 bits of the hash to be zero. About how many hashes are expected per solution?
explanation: Each hash succeeds with probability 2⁻²⁰, so about 2²⁰ ≈ 1.05 million tries. A billion is 2³⁰.
concept: Expected tries = 2^k for k zero bits.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: The last 2,016 Bitcoin blocks took 10 days instead of 14. How does difficulty change?
explanation: New difficulty = old × (expected / actual) = 14/10 = 1.4. Faster blocks mean higher difficulty.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Network hash rate doubles mid-epoch. Before retargeting, what is the average block interval?
explanation: Twice the hashing finds blocks twice as fast at the same target. Retargeting later restores 10 minutes.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A miner with 2% of network hash rate expects how many of 144 daily Bitcoin blocks?
explanation: 0.02 × 144 = 2.88 blocks a day on average. Actual counts vary with the Poisson process.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How many Ethereum epochs occur per day?
explanation: An epoch lasts 32 × 12 = 384 s, and 86,400 / 384 = 225. 7,200 is the number of slots per day.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: About how long does Ethereum finality take under normal conditions?
explanation: A checkpoint finalizes once the next one is justified, about two epochs. One slot is only inclusion; six blocks is a Bitcoin rule of thumb.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What fraction of staked ETH must be slashable before a finalized checkpoint can be reverted?
explanation: Two conflicting finalized checkpoints each need 2/3 support, so at least 1/3 of validators must have voted for both. Casper FFG makes that equivocation slashable.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A 4-node bank network uses Raft. One node is hacked and sends conflicting messages. What happens?
options: Raft offers no guarantee; it assumes crash faults only
Raft detects and removes the liar
The ledger stays safe because 3 of the 4 nodes are honest
explanation: Raft tolerates stopped nodes, not lying ones. Byzantine behaviour needs a BFT protocol with signatures and 3f + 1 replicas.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A validator ran the same key on a primary and a backup server and both signed. What follows?
explanation: Two signatures for one duty are provable equivocation. Operators must ensure a key is live in exactly one place.
concept: Never run one validator key twice.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why is 'kWh per transaction' misleading for Bitcoin?
options: Energy is spent per block, not per transaction
Fees pay for the miners' electricity directly per transaction
explanation: Hashing cost is the same whether a block holds 1 or 3,000 transactions, and batching packs many payments into one. The ratio is an average, not a marginal cost.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: If one consensus client runs on 70% of validators and has a bug, what is the danger?
options: It could finalize an invalid chain
Only that client's users lose rewards
explanation: Above 2/3, a single client's bug can carry finality with it. Client diversity keeps any one bug below the finality threshold.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which property can be sacrificed temporarily during a network partition without endangering safety?
explanation: A safe protocol may stall rather than finalize conflicting states. Giving up agreement would split the ledger.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which consensus best suits 20 known hospitals sharing records?
options: Anonymous DPoS voting by token holders
explanation: Known, vetted members can use identities and efficient ordering instead of costly Sybil resistance. Public PoW wastes energy and exposes data.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A startup claims its PoS chain is 'immune to 51% attacks'. Best assessment?
options: Wrong: PoS is weaker than any PoW chain under every model
Wrong: majority stake can still censor and attack, at the cost of slashing
Right: PoS has no attack threshold
explanation: PoS changes the resource from hash power to stake but keeps thresholds (1/3 for finality, 2/3 for control). Slashing raises the cost; it does not remove the risk.
concept: Every consensus has an attack threshold.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A small PoW coin shares Bitcoin's SHA-256 algorithm. What is its biggest risk?
options: It cannot adjust difficulty when hash rate changes
Rented Bitcoin hash power could easily overwhelm it
explanation: A tiny share of Bitcoin's hash power exceeds the small chain's total, enabling cheap 51% attacks. The algorithm itself is sound.
concept: Minority-hash chains are cheap to attack.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Design consensus for an IoT network of thousands of low-power devices doing micro-payments. Which fits best?
options: Full Ethereum validators on every sensor
A DAG-style or delegated scheme with lightweight validation by devices
A single central database with no replication across sites
explanation: Low-power devices cannot mine or stake 32 ETH; lightweight approval schemes such as a DAG, or delegation to gateways, fit. Central databases lose the shared-ledger benefits.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What issues X.509 identities to members of a Fabric network?
options: Each organisation's certificate authority, validated by its MSP
Miners on the public chain, who sign each member's key
explanation: Each organisation's CA issues certificates and its MSP defines which are valid. Orderers only sequence transactions.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is a Fabric channel?
options: A private ledger shared by a subset of members
The public Bitcoin network bridged into Fabric
explanation: Each channel has its own ledger, so non-members cannot see its transactions. Private Data Collections add finer privacy inside a channel.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does Fabric's world state hold?
options: The current value of every key
explanation: The world state is a database of latest values; the blockchain log keeps full history. Together they form the ledger.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Name Fabric's transaction flow.
explanation: Endorsers execute first, orderers sequence, peers validate and commit. Classic blockchains order before executing.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why must chaincode be deterministic?
options: So miners can verify the proof of work in each block
Endorsers must produce identical read-write sets
explanation: Random numbers, clocks or API calls give different results on different peers and endorsements fail to match. Determinism is about agreement, not speed.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the chaincode lifecycle order?
explanation: Each organisation installs and approves; once enough approve, the definition is committed to the channel. Mining and staking are not part of Fabric.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which model assigns permissions to roles rather than individuals?
explanation: Role-based access control gives users roles, and roles carry permissions. DAC lets owners grant rights directly.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In which model does a central authority assign security labels and clearances?
explanation: Mandatory access control enforces system-wide labels that users cannot override. DAC leaves decisions to resource owners.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What characterises discretionary access control?
options: Permissions are tied only to job roles defined by HR
Labels set by a central authority
Resource owners decide who may access their objects
explanation: DAC, as in typical file systems, lets owners grant and revoke rights. Its weakness is that owners may share too widely.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
options: Authentication grants permissions; authorisation then logs them
Authentication proves identity; authorisation decides permitted actions
explanation: Fabric authenticates with X.509 certificates and authorises through policies and chaincode checks. Authorisation without authentication is meaningless.
concept: Who are you vs what may you do.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does a Private Data Collection put on the shared ledger?
options: The data encrypted with a public key
Only a hash of the private data
explanation: Authorised peers hold the data; everyone else sees the hash as evidence. This keeps confidential terms off the channel ledger.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the principle of least privilege?
options: Give users the same rights as owners
Grant all permissions to administrators and trusted staff
Deny every request by default forever
Grant only the permissions needed for the task
explanation: Minimal rights limit damage from mistakes or compromise. RBAC supports it by scoping each role.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Endorsement policy OutOf(2, 'A.peer', 'B.peer', 'C.peer'). Which set satisfies it?
options: Endorsements from A and an orderer
explanation: Any two of the three organisations suffice. Orderers do not endorse.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Policy AND('Pharma.peer', 'Cargo.peer'). A transaction has endorsements from Pharma and Hospital. Result?
explanation: The policy needs both Pharma and Cargo specifically; Hospital cannot substitute. Committing peers mark it invalid.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Two transactions in one block both read key K at version 5 and write it. What happens to the second?
options: Both succeed and K is overwritten twice
It fails MVCC and is marked invalid
explanation: After the first commits, K's version changes, so the second's read set is stale. Fabric invalidates it rather than re-running.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Chaincode reads the system clock to timestamp a record. What is the likely outcome?
options: Endorsements differ and the transaction fails
The world state stores both times
It works, because peer clocks are synchronised by NTP
explanation: Peers' clocks differ slightly, producing different write sets. Use the transaction timestamp from the proposal instead.
concept: Use tx timestamp, not local clock.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Only QA officers may call ReleaseBatch(). Which check belongs in the chaincode?
options: Verify the caller's certificate carries role=QA_Officer
Check the caller's IP address against the QA office range
explanation: Fabric exposes the client identity and its attributes to chaincode for RBAC checks. IPs and fees are not identity.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: The vaccine batch is IN_TRANSIT. Which call should chaincode reject?
options: A read of the batch status
explanation: Release must precede transit; the state machine only allows IN_TRANSIT → RECEIVED next. Reads change nothing.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Under MAC with Bell–LaPadula rules, can a 'Secret' user read a 'Top Secret' file?
options: Yes, if the user is an administrator
Yes, if the owner allows it
explanation: Clearance must dominate the object's label to read. Owners cannot override mandatory labels.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A clinician shares patient files with a friend using owner rights. Which model allowed this, and what is the risk?
options: DAC; owners can leak data beyond policy
MAC; the labels were set too strictly
explanation: DAC trusts owners' judgement, so data can spread outside policy. MAC prevents owner-driven sharing of labelled data.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: One user both raises and approves purchase orders. Which control is missing?
explanation: Splitting conflicting duties across roles stops one person committing fraud alone. RBAC can enforce it with mutually exclusive roles.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why does Fabric execute transactions before ordering them?
options: To catch non-determinism and conflicts before commit, in parallel
To make every peer run every contract before ordering
explanation: Endorsers simulate in parallel and only consistent results are ordered and validated. Ordering still exists.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A competitor on the same channel should not see agreed prices. What is the best Fabric feature?
options: A Private Data Collection for the parties
A new public channel for everyone
explanation: A PDC shares data only with listed organisations and puts a hash on the channel. Endorsement policy governs approval, not visibility.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why should personal data stay off an immutable ledger?
options: It cannot be erased if a deletion right is exercised
Chaincode cannot read personal data stored in world state
explanation: Immutability conflicts with erasure rights, so store PII off-chain with a hash or reference on-chain.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which Fabric component orders transactions but does not execute chaincode?
explanation: Orderers sequence endorsed transactions into blocks. Endorsers execute; MSPs validate identities.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A hospital nurse role must read records but never modify them. Which RBAC grant fits?
explanation: Least privilege gives exactly the needed read access. Write or owner rights exceed the need.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Validation detects an endorsement policy failure. What happens to the transaction?
options: It is deleted from the block
It updates state with a warning flag
It stays in the block but is marked invalid, without updating state
It is re-sent to endorsers automatically for a fresh simulation
explanation: Fabric records invalid transactions for audit but skips their writes. Nothing is re-executed automatically.
concept: Invalid txs are recorded, not applied.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A consortium wants all members to see all data and settle disputes by a public blockchain instead of Fabric. Best assessment?
options: Impossible: public chains cannot store any consortium data at all
Possible, but loses confidentiality and identity controls Fabric offers
explanation: Public chains provide openness but expose data and lack member identity and private channels. The choice depends on confidentiality needs.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A ministry wants document access controlled by classification levels that officers cannot override. Which model and why?
options: RBAC alone, since job roles are enough
MAC, because labels are centrally enforced
explanation: Classified material needs mandatory labels and clearances; DAC lets owners leak. RBAC may complement but does not enforce levels.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Design the endorsement policy for vaccine custody transfer between manufacturer, carrier and hospital. Which is soundest?
options: Any single organisation may endorse, as long as the orderer accepts
No endorsement policy, rely on MVCC
Require the current custodian and the receiving party to both endorse
explanation: Both sides of a handover must agree, preventing unilateral claims. MVCC handles conflicts, not authorisation.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Euler's theorem generalises Fermat's: for gcd(a, n) = 1,
explanation: For prime n, φ(n) = n − 1 and this is Fermat's theorem. It underpins RSA correctness.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is φ(n) for n = p·q with distinct primes?
explanation: Totient is multiplicative for coprime factors, and φ(p) = p − 1. pq − 1 is φ only when n is prime.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why is RSA decryption correct?
options: Decryption uses the hash of M to cancel the exponent
e·d ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)) and Euler's theorem gives M^(ed) ≡ M
explanation: M^(ed) = M^(1 + kφ(n)) = M·(M^φ(n))^k ≡ M. n is composite by design.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: In Miller–Rabin, what is a 'strong liar'?
options: A prime that fails the test
A base that makes a composite pass the test
A base that proves a prime number to be composite
explanation: Some bases wrongly report 'probably prime' for a composite. At most a quarter of bases lie, so repeated rounds help.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How many multiplications does square-and-multiply add beyond squarings?
options: One per bit in total, ones and zeros
One per 1 bit in the exponent
explanation: Every bit squares; only 1 bits also multiply. Hence e = 65537 (two 1 bits) is fast.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why can 6 have no inverse modulo 15?
explanation: A common factor means 6x is always a multiple of 3 mod 15, never 1. Modulus primality is not required, only coprimality.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which algorithm is fastest for factoring large RSA moduli?
explanation: GNFS is sub-exponential and holds factoring records. Miller–Rabin tests primality; BSGS solves discrete logs.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why is e = 65537 a popular RSA public exponent?
options: It removes the need for padding
It is prime with only two 1 bits, so encryption is fast
It is the largest exponent the standard allows
explanation: 65537 = 2¹⁶ + 1 needs 16 squarings and one multiply. Padding is still required.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does a Montgomery ladder do against timing attacks?
options: Shortens the private key so each step is quicker
Performs the same operations for every exponent bit
explanation: Uniform work per bit removes data-dependent timing. Random delays only add noise.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Two moduli used in CRT must be:
explanation: Coprimality guarantees a unique combined solution. 4 and 9 work although neither is prime.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Signing in RSA uses which key?
explanation: Signature s = H(M)^d mod n; anyone verifies with e. Using a public key to sign would let anyone forge.
concept: Sign with d, verify with e.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which test can be fooled by Carmichael numbers for all coprime bases?
explanation: Carmichael numbers satisfy a^(n−1) ≡ 1 for all coprime a. Miller–Rabin catches them by checking square roots of 1.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is 3^100 mod 7?
explanation: 3^6 ≡ 1 and 100 ≡ 4 (mod 6), so 3^4 = 81 ≡ 4. 1 assumes 100 is a multiple of 6.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

stem: Solve x ≡ 1 (mod 4), x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5).
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: p = 5, q = 11, e = 3. What is d?
explanation: φ = 40 and 3·27 = 81 = 2·40 + 1. 13 is a ciphertext value, not d.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Public key (e, n) = (3, 55). Encrypt M = 7.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Key (e, n) = (3, 33) with d = 7. Decrypt C = 31.
explanation: 31⁷ mod 33 = 4, and 4³ = 64 ≡ 31 confirms it. 7 is d, not the plaintext.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: For n = 25 and base a = 7, Miller–Rabin gives b₀ = 18, b₁ = 24. What does it report?
options: Probably prime, so 7 is a strong liar for 25
The test cannot start because 25 is odd
explanation: b₁ ≡ −1 (mod 25) ends the round with 'probably prime', yet 25 = 5². Base 2 instead gives 8, 14, 21 and exposes it.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Write n − 1 = 2^k·m for n = 97.
explanation: 96 = 32·3, so k = 5 and m = 3 (odd). m must be an odd integer.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How many squarings and multiplications does square-and-multiply need for exponent 13 (1101₂)?
explanation: Four bits give four squarings, and three 1 bits give three multiplies. Naive repeated multiplication uses 12.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An RSA modulus n = 323 leaks φ(n) = 288. What are p and q?
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Two users share modulus n but use different e. Why is this dangerous?
options: Signatures become longer because the moduli collide
Either user can factor n from their own d and read the other's messages
explanation: Knowing any (e, d) pair for n allows factoring n, exposing everyone using it. Each user needs a unique n.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: You find 34² ≡ 1² (mod 77). Which factor does gcd(34 − 1, 77) reveal?
explanation: 34² = 1156 = 15·77 + 1, and 34 ≢ ±1, so gcd(33, 77) = 11 is a proper factor; gcd(35, 77) gives 7. 33 is x − y itself.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A device decrypts faster for some ciphertexts. Which defence removes the dependence on the ciphertext?
options: Caching common results so repeated inputs run faster
Blinding with a fresh random r each time
explanation: Blinding randomises the value exponentiated so timing no longer correlates with the attacker's input. Key length does not affect leakage.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why must RSA signatures sign a hash with proper padding rather than the raw message?
options: Raw RSA is malleable: signatures multiply into forgeries
Raw messages cannot be exponentiated modulo n
explanation: s₁·s₂ is a valid signature on m₁·m₂ for textbook RSA. Hash-and-pad schemes such as RSA-PSS block this.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A legacy system uses 1,024-bit RSA for new certificates in 2026. Best verdict?
options: Inadequate: migrate to at least 2,048-bit RSA or ECC
Adequate for another decade with e = 65537
explanation: 1,024-bit RSA no longer meets standards; 2,048-bit RSA or 256-bit ECC are current minimums. e does not affect factoring difficulty.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A key generator runs one Miller–Rabin round per candidate. Assessment?
options: Too weak: run many rounds to push error below 2⁻⁸⁰
Excessive: use trial division to be fully certain
explanation: One round can err with probability up to 1/4. Standards require dozens of rounds or proven tests.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: You must sign firmware updates for millions of IoT devices that verify on tiny chips. Which design is best?
options: Ed25519 or ECDSA signatures with a hardware-protected signing key
A shared HMAC key embedded in every device's firmware
explanation: Public-key signatures let devices verify without holding signing secrets; ECC keeps verification light. A shared HMAC key in every device lets any extracted key forge updates.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does an eavesdropper on Diffie–Hellman see?
options: The secrets a and b, but not the key
p, g, g^a mod p and g^b mod p
explanation: Only public parameters and half-keys cross the channel. Computing the key from them is the Diffie–Hellman problem.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the computational Diffie–Hellman (CDH) problem?
options: Finding a from g^a and the prime p
Computing g^(ab) from g^a and g^b
explanation: CDH asks for the shared key directly; solving the DLP solves CDH. Finding a from g^a is the DLP itself.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does ElGamal's y₁ = α^k serve as?
options: A hash of the plaintext used to check integrity
An ephemeral DH share that lets Bob rebuild the mask
explanation: Bob raises y₁ to his secret a to obtain β^k, the mask on y₂. y₂ carries the message.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What does 'double-and-add' compute?
explanation: It is square-and-multiply in additive notation: double for each bit, add P on 1 bits.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What is the collision-resistance level of SHA-256?
explanation: Birthday attacks halve the exponent: 2^(256/2). 2²⁵⁶ is the preimage bound.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: How many quadratic residues are there among 1 … 22 modulo 23?
explanation: Exactly (p − 1)/2 non-zero values are squares. 12 would exceed half.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why is the group order of a curve important?
options: Security depends on its largest prime factor
It decides the hash length used in signatures
explanation: Pohlig–Hellman reduces the ECDLP to the prime factors of the order, so a large prime subgroup is needed. Order equal to p is actually a weak (anomalous) case.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Why is the DH result usually passed through a key-derivation function?
options: To hide it from the other party
To turn the group element into uniform symmetric keys
To make it shorter for storage
To add authentication to the exchange automatically
explanation: Group elements are not uniformly random bit strings; a KDF such as HKDF extracts and expands keys. A KDF does not authenticate.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Hasse's theorem bounds the number of points N on a curve over F_p as:
explanation: The count stays close to p + 1. This is why curve order roughly matches field size.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: For the same security level, ECC public keys compared with RSA are:
explanation: 256-bit ECC matches 3,072-bit RSA. Smaller keys save bandwidth and storage.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: What property does ElGamal have that textbook RSA lacks?
options: No need for a private key to decrypt
explanation: A fresh k per message makes ciphertexts differ. ElGamal ciphertexts are actually longer.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which attack solves a DLP in roughly √p time with little memory?
explanation: Pollard's rho matches BSGS's time but needs almost no memory. BSGS needs √p storage.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: p = 23, g = 5. Alice's secret a = 6. What does she send?
explanation: 5⁶ = 15,625 ≡ 8 (mod 23). 19 is Bob's value with b = 15.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: p = 23, g = 5, a = 6, b = 15, so A = 8 and B = 19. What is the shared key?
explanation: 19⁶ ≡ 8¹⁵ ≡ 2 (mod 23). 8 and 19 are the public values.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: p = 23, α = 5, Bob's secret a = 6. What is β?
explanation: β = 5⁶ mod 23 = 8. 10 is y₁ for k = 3.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: With β = 8, k = 3, x = 10 and p = 23, what is y₂ = x·β^k mod p?
explanation: 8³ = 512 ≡ 6, and 10·6 = 60 ≡ 14. 60 is unreduced.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Bob receives (y₁, y₂) = (10, 14) with a = 6, p = 23. What is x?
explanation: y₁^a = 10⁶ ≡ 6, its inverse is 4, and 14·4 = 56 ≡ 10. 6 is the mask.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Solving 2^x ≡ 21 (mod 29) with BSGS, what is m?
explanation: √29 ≈ 5.39, so m = 6. Five would cover only 25 exponents.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Is 10 a quadratic residue mod 23? (10^11 mod 23 = 22)
options: Yes, because the result is non-zero
explanation: Euler's criterion gives −1 for non-residues. Non-zero alone tells nothing.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Which value is a quadratic residue mod 17: 6 or 13? (6⁸ ≡ 16, 13⁸ ≡ 1)
explanation: 13⁸ ≡ 1 marks a residue; 6⁸ ≡ 16 ≡ −1 marks a non-residue. Indeed 8² = 64 ≡ 13.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Curve y² = x³ + 2x + 2 over F₁₇. Is it non-singular?
explanation: 4a³ + 27b² = 32 + 108 = 140 = 8·17 + 4 ≠ 0. b ≠ 0 alone proves nothing.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: On y² = x³ + 2x + 2 over F₁₇, doubling G = (5, 1) gives λ = 13. What is 2G?
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: G = (5, 1) on y² = x³ + 2x + 2 over F₁₇ has order 19. What is 19G and 20G?
explanation: Order 19 means 19G = O, so 20G = O + G = G. Scalars reduce mod 19.
concept: kG depends on k mod order.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: That curve has 19 points including O. Why is G = (5, 1) a generator?
options: All curves are cyclic, with (5, 1) as a standard generator
19 is prime, so every non-identity point has order 19
explanation: By Lagrange, orders divide 19, so non-O points have order 19. Within Hasse's bound, 19 ≤ 17 + 1 + 2√17.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A 64-bit hash is used for file deduplication across a huge archive. When do collisions become likely?
explanation: Birthday bound √(2⁶⁴) = 2³². Large archives reach that scale, so use 128+ bit hashes.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Alice and Bob run DH with p = 23, g = 5, but g's order is only 22. Mallory forces g' = 22 (order 2). What happens?
options: The key can only be 1 or 22, so it is trivial to guess
The protocol becomes more secure against eavesdroppers
explanation: A small-order generator confines the key to a tiny subgroup. Validate parameters and use prime-order subgroups.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: An implementation accepts a peer's point without checking it lies on the curve. Which attack does this enable?
options: Birthday collision on SHA-256 used in the handshake
Invalid-curve attack leaking the private scalar
explanation: Points on weaker curves let an attacker recover the secret modulo small orders. Always validate received points.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A bank wants post-quantum safety and asks whether moving RSA-2048 to ECC-256 achieves it. Best answer?
options: No: only symmetric keys are at risk from quantum computers
No: Shor's algorithm breaks both; plan for post-quantum schemes
Yes, if keys double in size
explanation: Shor's algorithm solves factoring and discrete logs, including ECDLP. Post-quantum schemes such as lattice-based KEMs are the path.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: A protocol reuses one static DH key for years and logs all traffic. Assessment?
options: Poor: a later key compromise decrypts all past traffic
Good: static keys save computation and simplify audits
Fine because DH keys cannot leak
explanation: Without ephemeral keys there is no forward secrecy. Ephemeral ECDHE limits damage to one session.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)

subject: Blockchain & Access Control
stem: Design a wallet key-management scheme for many addresses from one backup. Which is best?
options: Hierarchical deterministic keys from one seed, with the seed stored offline
One key reused for every address
A fresh unrelated key per address, never backed up for safety
Keys derived from the user's password alone
explanation: HD wallets derive many keys from a single seed, so one offline backup restores all while addresses stay distinct. Password-only derivation invites brute force.
concept: HD wallet from an offline seed.
source: Course notes, Blockchain & Access Control (IIT Bhubaneswar M.Tech)
